goals: State where a member declared private, default, protected or public can be accessed
Read and predict the result of access to members from another class of the same package
Explain how private data with public methods achieves encapsulation
Write getter and setter methods that validate a value before it is stored

slides.heading: Encapsulation and access specifiers
slides.body_md: Part 1: **encapsulation**, the four **access specifiers**, the **visibility table**, and **getters and setters** that guard private data.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: encapsulation, the four access specifiers, the visibility table, private in action, getters and setters, validation and read-only data
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to encapsulation. In this part we learn how a class protects its data. We meet the four access specifiers, private, default, protected and public, and the table that tells which code may use a member. We watch the compiler refuse private access, and we write getter and setter methods that check a value before it is stored. We also build read only data.

slides.heading: Data and methods, wrapped together
slides.body_md: **Encapsulation** binds the data members and the methods that use them into one class and **hides the data**. Other classes reach the data only through the **public methods** of the class.

visual.caption: The boundary of the class: other classes reach the private data only through its public methods.

slides.narration: Encapsulation means two things. First, the data and the methods that work on it are placed together in one class. Second, the data is hidden: it is made private, so other classes cannot touch it directly. They have to ask the public methods of the class. In the picture, the boundary stops the direct arrow, and the public methods are the doors.

slides.heading: The four access specifiers
slides.body_md: An **access specifier** decides which code may use a member. It is written before the data member, method or constructor. When none is written, the member has **default** (package) access.

rows: the narrowest: its own class only
its own class and the same package

visual.alt: Table of the four access specifiers: private for its own class only, default with no keyword for the same package, protected for the package and subclasses, and public for every class

slides.narration: An access specifier decides which code may use a member of a class. Java has four levels. Private is the narrowest. If no specifier is written, the member has default access, which is also called package access. Protected is wider, and public is the widest. The same specifiers can be written before data members, methods and constructors.

slides.heading: private: only inside its own class

rows: coins has private access in Gullak
coins has private access in Gullak
audit() has private access in Gullak

visual.alt: Table of three refused statements: reading coins gives coins has private access in Gullak, writing coins gives coins has private access in Gullak and calling audit gives audit() has private access in Gullak
visual.caption: All three errors appear at compile time, before the program runs.

slides.narration: A private member can be used only by code written inside its own class. Here the class Check is a different class, even though it is in the same file. Reading coins gives a compile time error that says coins has private access in Gullak. Writing to coins gives the same message, and calling the private method audit gives a similar one. All these errors appear at compile time.

slides.heading: The visibility table
slides.body_md: Learn this table. Inheritance is not part of this chapter: for **protected**, only the rule about subclasses is needed.

visual.alt: Visibility table: private is accessible in the same class only; default in the same class and the same package; protected in the same class, the same package and subclasses in other packages; public everywhere
visual.caption: Moving down the table, the access only widens.

slides.narration: This table is worth learning by heart. Private members are open only to their own class. Default members are open to the same package as well. Protected members are open to the same package and also to subclasses, even in other packages. Public members are open to every class. Moving down the table, the access only widens. Inheritance is not in this chapter, so only the rule for subclasses is needed.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which statements compile?

compile-time error: audit() has private access in Gullak

visual.alt: Table of six uses of Gullak members from another class of the same package: g.coins (private) gives compile-time error: coins has private access in Gullak; g.notes (default) gives 5; g.seals (protected) gives 2; g.slots (public) gives 1; g.total() (public method) gives 90; g.audit() (private method) gives compile-time error: audit() has private access in Gullak

slides.narration: Let us test every level from the class Check. Reading notes, which has default access, displays five. Reading seals, which is protected, displays two, because Check is in the same package. Reading slots, which is public, displays one. The public method total displays ninety. But the private coins and the private method audit are refused by the compiler.

That means we can show private access being refused, and default, protected and public access being allowed inside the package. We cannot show a subclass in another package, so for that case we only state the rule from the table. We never pretend that a demonstration has run when it has not.

rows: sales has private access in Stall

visual.alt: Table: inside the class Stall the private sales of another object can be read and beats gives true; in the class Market, a.sales gives sales has private access in Stall
visual.caption: Access is decided by the class in which the code is written, not by the object.

slides.narration: Private access is decided by the class, not by the object. In the class Stall, the method beats reads the private sales of another Stall object, and this is allowed because the method is written inside the class. The program prints true. But the class Market cannot read a dot sales: the compiler says sales has private access in Stall.

slides.heading: Public methods: the doors of the class
slides.body_md: Private data needs public methods to be useful. An **accessor** (getter) reads a value. A **mutator** (setter) changes it, and can **check** the new value first.

rows: returns the value of a private member; changes nothing
changes a private member, usually after a check

visual.alt: Table of accessor and mutator methods: the getter returns a private value and changes nothing; the setter changes a private value, usually after a check; examples getReading and setReading of the class Thermo

slides.narration: Private data is useful only when the class offers public methods. An accessor, also called a getter, returns a value and changes nothing. A mutator, also called a setter, changes the value. The great advantage is that a setter can check the new value before storing it. The class Thermo has one of each, getReading and setReading.

slides.heading: A setter that validates

nodes.label: Yes: reading is set to t

visual.alt: Flow of the setter: setReading is called, the range from minus 10 to 55 is tested, a valid value is stored and an invalid one gives a message and leaves the old reading
visual.caption: The setter is the gatekeeper of the private data.

slides.narration: Here is the class Thermo. The reading is private. The setter tests whether the new value lies from minus ten to fifty five. If it does, the reading is stored. If not, the setter prints a message and the old reading stays. Because no other code can write the reading, the object can never hold an impossible temperature.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: three readings

visual.alt: Table of three separate readings given to a new Thermo object: setReading 31.5 then getReading gives 31.5; setReading 80 then getReading gives Rejected: 80.0 / 0.0; setReading -20 then getReading gives Rejected: -20.0 / 0.0
visual.caption: A new Thermo object starts with the default reading 0.0.

slides.narration: We give three readings, each to a new Thermo object. Thirty one point five is inside the range, so it is stored and the getter returns it. Eighty is outside the range, so the setter prints Rejected, and the getter returns the starting value, zero point zero. Minus twenty is also outside the range and is rejected in the same way.

slides.body_md: Choose the correct result.
slides.narration: Remember what the compiler does when another class touches a private member.

slides.heading: Without encapsulation

rows: reading has private access in Thermo
private data and a checking setter

visual.alt: Table comparing three designs: a public data member accepts 80 and prints 80.0; a private member refuses direct assignment with reading has private access in Thermo; a private member with a checking setter refuses the value with a message

slides.narration: See what happens without encapsulation. In the class Raw the reading is public, so any class can assign eighty and the object accepts it without complaint. In the class Thermo the reading is private, so the same assignment is refused by the compiler. The setter does allow a controlled change, and it refuses eighty with a message.

slides.heading: Read-only data and private constructors
slides.body_md: **Private data with only a getter** is read-only for other classes. A **private constructor** cannot be used to create objects from other classes.

rows: no such method: cannot find symbol
badgeNo has private access in Badge
Mint() has private access in Mint

visual.alt: Table for the class Badge, which has a private number and only a getter: the getter prints 214; a setter call gives cannot find symbol; direct assignment gives badgeNo has private access in Badge; a private constructor gives Mint() has private access in Mint
visual.caption: Private data and a getter only: the attribute is read-only for other classes.

slides.narration: If a class has a private number and only a getter, other classes can read the number but not change it. A call of a setter that was never written gives cannot find symbol, and direct assignment is refused. Constructors can be private too. Then another class cannot create an object with new, and the compiler says that the constructor has private access.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the Piggy savings box

visual.alt: Trace table of the Piggy savings box: after deposit 250 the amount is 250; after deposit minus 40 it is 250; after deposit 100 it is 350

slides.narration: The Piggy class keeps the rupees private. The method deposit adds an amount only when it is positive. After a deposit of two hundred fifty, the amount is two hundred fifty. A deposit of minus forty is not positive, so it is ignored, and the amount stays the same. A deposit of one hundred then brings the amount to three hundred fifty.

slides.heading: Quick check: protected
slides.body_md: Decide on the assertion and the reason.
slides.narration: Recall which classes get access to a protected member, and test the statement against the visibility table.

slides.heading: Access for classes themselves
slides.body_md: A **top-level class** is either **public** or has default access. The levels private and protected are for members.

visual.alt: Table of modifiers before a top-level class: public and no modifier are accepted; private gives modifier private not allowed here, protected gives modifier protected not allowed here and static gives modifier static not allowed here
visual.caption: The levels private and protected are meant for the members of a class.

slides.narration: The access specifiers are meant mainly for members. A top level class can be public, or it can have no specifier, which means default access. Writing private or protected before a top level class is an error, and the compiler says that the modifier is not allowed here. The word static is not allowed there either.

slides.heading: Quick check: steps of encapsulation
slides.body_md: Arrange the steps in order.
slides.narration: Decide what must exist first, then which methods guard the data, and who uses them last.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: data and methods in one class; data hidden
private: class; default: package; protected: package and subclasses; public: all
refused by the compiler outside its class (class-wide, not object-wide)
private data with a getter only

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: encapsulation, the four specifiers, the visibility rule of each, private access being class-wide, getters and setters, and read-only data

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Encapsulation keeps data and methods together and hides the data. The four specifiers are private, default, protected and public, and the visibility table shows how far each one reaches. Private access is refused outside the class, but it is allowed for any object inside the class. Getters read, setters change and validate, and a getter alone makes the data read only.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn the visibility table: private is the class only, default adds the package, protected adds subclasses, public is everyone.
Name the rule when you explain an error: "a private member cannot be accessed outside its class".
In a program keep the data members `private` and give `public` methods; validate in the setter and in the constructor.
A default member has no keyword: do not write the word default before a member.
Say "accessor" or "getter" for a method that reads, and "mutator" or "setter" for a method that changes.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. Learn the visibility table: private is the class only, default adds the package, protected adds subclasses, and public is everyone. When you explain an error, name the rule, that a private member cannot be accessed outside its class. In programs, keep the data private, give public methods, and validate in the setter and in the constructor. A default member has no keyword.

decks.title: Scope and Lifetime of Variables
goals: Name the four kinds of variables and state where each is declared
Compare instance and static variables with programs
Explain the scope of argument and local variables and the effect of blocks
Identify the type and scope of each variable in a given program

slides.heading: Scope of variables
slides.body_md: Part 2: **instance**, **static**, **argument** and **local** variables, their **scope** and **lifetime**, hiding with **this**, and the static context.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the four kinds of variables, instance variables, static variables, argument variables, local variables and blocks, hiding and this, static context and lifetime
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part. Every variable in a program has a kind, a scope and a lifetime. We study instance variables, static variables, argument variables and local variables. We see how blocks limit the scope of a variable, how one name can hide another, why the main method cannot use an instance variable directly, and how long each kind of variable lives.

slides.heading: Four kinds of variables
slides.body_md: The **place** of the declaration, and the keyword **static**, decide the kind of a variable.

rows: in the class, outside methods, no static
the methods of the class, through an object
in the class, outside methods, with static
the whole class; through the class name elsewhere
in the header of a method or constructor
inside a method, constructor or block
its block, from the declaration onwards

visual.alt: Table of the four kinds of variables: instance variables with one copy for each object, static variables with one copy for the class, argument variables of a method header, and local variables inside a block, each with its scope

slides.narration: There are four kinds of variables. An instance variable is declared in the class, outside the methods, without the word static, and each object has its own copy. A static variable is declared with the word static and is shared by the whole class. An argument variable is declared in the header of a method. A local variable is declared inside a method or a block.

slides.heading: Spotting the kinds in a program

rows: declared with static in the class

visual.alt: Table of the variables of the class TokenDesk: next is static, token is an instance variable, counter is an argument variable of serve and wait is a local variable of serve

slides.narration: Look at the class TokenDesk. The variable next is declared with static, so it is a static variable. The variable token is in the class without static, so it is an instance variable. The variable counter is in the header of serve, so it is an argument variable. The variable wait is inside the body of serve, so it is a local variable.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: type and scope in a program

visual.alt: Table that classifies the variables of the Cafe program: served is static, price is an instance variable, p and qty are argument variables, and bill, c and amount are local variables; the program prints 60 4
visual.caption: The program prints 60 and 4.

slides.narration: Let us classify the variables of the Cafe program. The variable served has the word static, so it belongs to the class. The variable price is an instance variable. The names p and qty are argument variables, of the constructor and of order. The variable bill is local to order. The variables c and amount are local to main. The program prints sixty and four.

slides.heading: Instance variables: one copy for each object
slides.body_md: Every object has **its own copy** of an instance variable. Changing it in one object does not affect the others.

rows: each object has its own token
changing one copy leaves the other

visual.alt: Table of instance variables: three objects print their tokens 1 2 3; after a.token is set to 70 the objects print 70 2

slides.narration: An instance variable has one copy for each object. Three TokenDesk objects hold the tokens one, two and three. When we assign seventy to the token of a, the token of b is not touched, and it still holds two. Each copy is created with its object and is reached with the name of the object and a dot.

slides.heading: Static variables: one copy for the class
slides.body_md: A **static (class) variable** has **one copy** shared by all the objects. It is created when the class is loaded.

visual.caption: One static copy for the class; one instance copy for each object.

slides.narration: A static variable belongs to the class and has only one copy. In the picture the class holds the variable next, and the objects a and b hold one token each. The constructor copies next into the token and then increases next. So the objects get different tokens, but there is one shared counter, which now stands at three.

slides.body_md: What is the value of next?
slides.narration: Count how many times the constructor runs, and remember that there is one shared variable.

slides.heading: Reaching a static variable
slides.body_md: Use the **class name**: `TokenDesk.next`. It works even **before any object exists**. Through a reference it reaches the **same** single copy.

visual.alt: Table of the static variable next after 0, 1, 2 and 3 objects: 1, 2, 3, 4
visual.caption: The variable exists from the moment the class is loaded, even before the first object.

slides.narration: A static variable is reached by the class name and a dot. It exists as soon as the class is loaded, so it can be read before any object is created. The table shows the value after zero, one, two and three objects. The usual style is to write the class name, but a reference reaches the same single copy, so a change made through one reference is seen through every other.

slides.body_md: True or false?

slides.heading: Argument variables: copies of the values

visual.alt: Table of an argument variable: inside raise the copy m prints inside 15; in main the original m still prints outside 10
visual.caption: The method works on a copy.

slides.narration: An argument variable is created when the method is called, and it receives a copy of the value passed. In the program, raise adds five to its own copy of m, and prints fifteen. Back in main, the variable m still holds ten, because the two variables are different, although they have the same name. The argument variable ceases to exist when the method returns.

slides.heading: Local variables and blocks
slides.body_md: A **local variable** is known from its declaration to the closing brace of its **block**. A `for` variable belongs to the loop.

sections.heading: 1. Encapsulation and the access specifiers
sections.body_md:
**Encapsulation** is the binding of the data members and the methods that work on them in a class, with the data protected from direct access by other classes (data hiding). The way into the data is a set of public methods.

An **access specifier** is written before a member and decides which code may use it: **private**, **protected** and **public**; a member with none has **default** (package) access.

**Visibility**

| Member is | Same class | Same package | Subclass in another package | Any other class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| private | Yes | No | No | No |
| default | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| protected | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| public | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

key_terms.definition_md: The binding of data and methods in a class, with the data hidden from direct access outside the class.
A keyword (private, protected or public) that fixes where a member can be accessed; no keyword means default access.
The access of a member with no specifier: its own class and the classes of the same package.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing the visibility table wrongly: protected also includes the package, and default does not include subclasses in other packages.
- Making the data members public and then saying the class is encapsulated.
- Forgetting that a private member is accessible to every object of the same class, inside that class.
- Writing the word default before a member (a member with no specifier has default access).
- Using a loop variable or a block variable after its block.
- Using an instance variable directly in main.
- Assuming a static variable restarts for every object, or a local variable remembers its value from the last call.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Definitions: the key words (binding of data and methods, data hiding, one copy for the class).
- Differences: two points, each stated for both sides.
- Programs (15 marks): private data members and public methods, constructor, validation, static counter where asked, input and output, variable description or comments.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes encapsulation in Java?

options.text_md: Creating a new class from an existing class so that it reuses the members of the old one
Binding the data and the methods that use it into one class, and protecting the data from direct access by other classes
Using one method name for several different tasks with different parameter lists
Showing only the essential features of an object and leaving out the background details

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Binding the data and the methods that use it into one class, and protecting the data from direct access by other classes. Encapsulation puts data and methods together in one unit, the class, and controls how the data is reached. The other statements describe inheritance, method overloading (polymorphism) and data abstraction.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The data member balance is private and the methods that read and change it are public. Declare the data member private and write only a setter method for it
Declare the data member private and write only a getter method for it
Declare the data member protected and write no methods for it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Declare the data member private and write only a getter method for it. questions.stem_md: What is the chief advantage of keeping the data members of a class private and changing them through public methods?

options.text_md: The data members take up less memory

Each method can check a new value before it is stored

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Each method can check a new value before it is stored. When the only way in is a method, the class controls what is stored, for example by refusing a negative amount. Memory use and speed are not affected, and free access for every class is exactly what encapsulation prevents.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Encapsulation** is the binding of data and the methods that work on it into a single unit, the class, while the data is protected from direct access by other classes (data hiding).

The data members are declared **private**, so other classes cannot touch them. **Public** methods (getters, setters) are the only way in, and each can check a value first. questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a static (class) variable and an instance variable.
questions.solution_md: Two points of difference, each stated for both variables, earn the marks; an example is welcome.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Static (class) variable | Instance variable |
|---|---|
| Declared with the keyword static | Declared without static |
| One copy shared by all the objects of the class | A separate copy for every object |
| Created when the class is loaded and exists until the program ends | Created with the object and exists as long as the object does |

Example: after three TokenDesk objects, the static variable next is `4`, while the instance variables token of the three objects are `1 2 3`.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the scope of a variable? State the scope of a local variable and of an argument variable.
questions.solution_md: One mark for the meaning of scope and one for the scopes of the two kinds of variables.

answer.model_answer_md:
The **scope** of a variable is the part of the program in which the variable can be used.

A **local variable** can be used from its declaration to the end of the block in which it is declared. An **argument variable** can be used only inside the body of its method or constructor. Outside its scope a name is unknown: `i` used after its for loop gives "cannot find symbol".

questions.stem_md: The statement count++; is written in the static method main of a class that declares the instance variable count. Why does the compiler reject it? How can the error be removed?
questions.solution_md: One mark for the reason and one for a correct remedy.

answer.model_answer_md:
The compiler reports "non-static variable count cannot be referenced from a static context". An instance variable belongs to an object, but the static method main runs without any object, so it does not know whose count is meant.

The error is removed by creating an object and using its variable, as in `Visits v = new Visits(); v.count++;` (the program then displays `1`), or by declaring count static.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: a static method cannot use an instance variable directly; no object exists
Remedy: use an object, or make the variable static

questions.stem_md: A method has a parameter named level, and the class has a data member also named level. What happens to the data member when the statement level = level + 5; is executed in the method? How can the data member be reached?
questions.solution_md: One mark for the hiding of the data member by the parameter and one mark for this.level.

answer.model_answer_md:
The parameter hides the data member, so level means the parameter; the statement changes only the parameter and the data member keeps its value (the program with this error displays `10`, the initial value).

The data member is reached with the keyword **this**: `this.level = level + 5;` stores the new value in the data member (the output is then `25`).

marking_scheme.step: Parameter hides the data member; the data member is unchanged
this.level used to reach the data member

questions.stem_md: State the lifetime of a local variable, an instance variable and a static variable.
questions.solution_md: One mark for the lifetime of the local variable, one for the lifetimes of the instance and static variables.

answer.model_answer_md:
A **local variable** (and an argument variable) is created when its method is called and destroyed when the method returns, so every call starts afresh: in the Tally program the three calls of bump() return `1 1 1`, because the local variable starts at 0 each time.

An **instance variable** lives as long as its object. A **static variable** is created when the class is loaded and lives until the program ends.

marking_scheme.step: Local variable: from the call to the return of the method
Instance variable: life of the object; static variable: life of the program
